<explanation>
Below is a step-by-step guide for drawing a system design diagram of the Klavis AI project. We’ll treat it as a full-stack, microservices-based integration platform with SDKs, bots, an API gateway, dozens of independently deployable MCP servers, and connections to external third-party services.

1. Identify the Project Type and Purpose  
   • Full-stack open-source integration platform (“Klavis AI”)  
   • Provides:  
     – Client SDKs (Python, TypeScript)  
     – Bot apps (Discord, Slack, Web, WhatsApp)  
     – Microservice MCP servers (100+ individual integrations)  
     – CI/CD pipelines and code generation (via Fern)  
     – Documentation & examples  

2. Main Architectural Components  
   A. Client Layer  
      1. AI Agent / LLM or custom application  
      2. Klavis SDKs (Python `klavis` package, TS `klavis` npm module)  
      3. Bot Containers (Discord, Slack, Web, WhatsApp - in `mcp-clients/`)  
   B. API Layer  
      4. API Gateway or Router (generated via Fern, exposing REST/OpenAPI endpoints)  
      5. Authentication & OAuth endpoints  
   C. Microservices Layer  
      6. MCP Server Instances (each subfolder in `mcp_servers/` is a separate Dockerized microservice)  
         – Each runs its own HTTP server (Python, Node.js/TypeScript, Go)  
         – Implements a standardized MCP protocol (create instance, list tools, call tools)  
   D. External Services  
      7. Third-party APIs (Gmail, Google Drive, Airtable, GitHub, Slack, etc.)  
      8. OAuth providers (handle OAuth redirects, callbacks)  
   E. Infrastructure  
      9. Codegen & API definitions (Fern: `fern.config.json`, `generators.yml`)  
     10. CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions workflows for linting, SDK releases)  
     11. Documentation site & examples (Docs in `docs/`, Jupyter notebooks in `examples/`)  

3. Relationships & Data Flows  
   – AI Agent → SDK calls → API Gateway → MCP Server microservice → External service  
   – SDK initiates OAuth flows: API Gateway returns `oauthUrl`, user redirects, callback → MCP Server stores tokens  
   – For function-calling: LLM <→> SDK <→> MCP Server tools API <→> External API  
   – Bots (Discord/Slack) receive webhooks/events → local Bot app → SDK → MCP Server → external API → Bot responds  

4. Architectural Patterns & Principles  
   – Microservices per integration for isolation and scaling  
   – Monorepo for all servers+clients + codegen config  
   – Standardized MCP protocol across languages/platforms  
   – Separation of concerns:  
     • Clients (SDK & bots) vs API Gateway vs Server implementations  
     • Auth management centralized in MCP Servers  
   – Infrastructure as code: Dockerfiles in every service directory, GitHub Actions for CI/CD  

5. Relevant Technologies  
   – Python (FastAPI or Flask) for Python-based MCP Servers & Python SDK  
   – TypeScript/Node.js (Express, Cloudflare Workers, GraphQL) for many servers & TS SDK  
   – Go (GitHub MCP server implementation)  
   – Docker for containerization  
   – Fern codegen for API definitions and documentation  
   – GitHub Actions for linting, releases  
   – OpenAPI/SSE for streaming responses  

6. Diagram Layout Suggestions  
   • Arrange components in horizontal layers:  
     1. Top: User Applications/AI Agents & Bot UIs  
     2. Next: SDKs & Bot Apps (Python/TS)  
     3. API Gateway / OpenAPI layer  
     4. Microservices cluster (boxes for representative MCP servers)  
     5. External Services (cloud icons for Gmail, Slack, Salesforce, etc.)  
     6. Infrastructure (below or side): CI/CD pipelines, Fern codegen, docs site)  
   • Use distinct shapes or colors:  
     – Green for client-side (SDKs, bots)  
     – Blue for API Gateway / Router  
     – Teal for MCP Server microservices  
     – Orange for external third-party services  
     – Grey for infrastructure/CI/CD  

7. Diagram Elements to Include  
   – Clear labels: “Python SDK,” “TS SDK,” “API Gateway,” “YouTube MCP Server,” etc.  
   – Directional arrows with annotations: e.g., “HTTP POST /create_server_instance,” “OAuth redirect → /callback,” “tool_call function.”  
   – Color coding per layer/type (see above)  
   – Notes on multi-tool workflows: show two microservices in parallel, combined tool list → back into one LLM conversation  

8. Tailoring the Diagram  
   – Emphasize SDK ↔ MCP Server separation for a full-stack integration platform  
   – Highlight microservice containers for each integration type  
   – Show OAuth flow arrows for services requiring user auth  
   – If documenting self-hosting, annotate Docker build & run steps per service  

By following these guidelines, you will produce a comprehensive, accurate system design diagram that reflects Klavis AI’s modular client/server architecture, integration-focused microservices, and supporting infrastructure. Make sure each component is distinctly labeled, use arrows to illustrate request/response flows, and apply consistent color-coding to differentiate layers.
